title: Manual chunk — deterministic core
description: Output of the ETL pipeline. Every field is derivable from source HTML by regex, href parsing or structural traversal. Page-level metadata (url, title, publication and amendment dates) lives on the page record and is joined at query time — see page.schema.json. Nothing here may be produced by a language model.

chunk_ref.description: Stable address, and the id. Do not add a separate opaque id: a sequential id is a citation that breaks silently when a paragraph is inserted upstream.

page_ref.description: FK to the page record. Everything page-level is joined from there rather than copied here.

text.description: Verbatim, whitespace-normalised. No summarisation or reordering — this is what gets quoted back.

heading_path.description: Full ancestry, outermost first. Prepended to the text when the chunk enters a prompt so it is self-describing. The leaf heading is the last element; do not store it separately.

ordinal.description: Position within the page. Gives you previous/next by arithmetic, so adjacency needs no stored pointers.

content_hash.description: Of the normalised text. Drives selective re-embedding — without it every crawl re-embeds the whole corpus.

kind.description: 'landing' marks Relevant Legislation pages, which are mappings not prose and should usually be excluded from applicant-facing answers.

heading_source.description: How the leaf of 'heading_path' was found. 'markup' is an h2-h4, which is the Manual asserting the boundary itself. 'emphasis' is a bold paragraph opening with a number that extends the page's own, promoted to a heading because 456 of the Manual's numbered subsections are set that way and cutting on markup alone left 39% of the corpus text with no heading at all. null is the prose above a page's first heading. This is the only field in the pipeline recording an inference, and it exists so that a consumer wanting strictly the Manual's own structure can filter to 'markup' and know what it gave up.

fragment.description: Present only when an over-long section was split on paragraph boundaries.

provisions.description: Statutory references. This is the filtering mechanism, so it carries how each edge was found.

id.description: Instrument and root are both parseable from this — TMA1995/s44(3)(a) yields instrument TMA1995 and root TMA1995/s44. Derive them in SQL as generated columns rather than storing them. Each dotted component may carry a letter suffix: the Regulations number a Part 3A, so 'reg 3A.3' is TMR1995/r3A.3, and an inserted regulation is r21.21A.

extraction.description: 'href' means the Manual's authors hyperlinked this provision, so the edge is near-certain; 'regex' means the extractor read it out of the prose, so it is an inference. Only href edges should hydrate primary law into an answer. TWO URL vocabularies count as href, not one: an AustLII consol_act/consol_reg node, which carries the address in its path, and a TimeBase '?id=tmact:217a', which carries it in a query string. Both are the authors stating what the passage is about, which is the only thing this field has ever distinguished. Before ingest/0.11.0 only AustLII was read and the corpus's 101 TimeBase anchors reached the snapshot through the prose alone — see SOURCE_NOTES.md §35, which also records why Federal Register links are deliberately NOT read: they name an instrument rather than a provision, and 475 of them resolve to 9 boilerplate URLs. A consumer wanting specifically AustLII-backed edges can still filter, because every href is verbatim in 'links'.

certainty.description: For regex edges. 'explicit' = instrument named adjacent. 'default' = bare 'section N', assumed Trade Marks Act. 'ambiguous' = several instruments in scope, e.g. 'section 26 of the Act' in a paragraph about the 1955 Act. Route ambiguous to review; never hydrate from it.

mention.description: Surface form. Keep while building — it is how you debug a bad edge. Droppable once the extractor is stable.

internal_refs.description: Manual-internal cross references, resolved to chunk or page refs, and carrying how each was found. Unresolvable targets are dropped, not guessed. A ref equal to this chunk's own page_ref is kept, not filtered: it means the target is elsewhere on this same page, which tells a retrieval layer to offer a sibling chunk rather than another page. One record per target — a passage that both links to a page and names it in prose asserts one edge, and the hyperlink is the stronger evidence for it.

ref.description: The target, as a page_ref or a chunk_ref.

extraction.description: The same distinction 'provisions' draws, and it is load-bearing for the same reason: an href is the Manual's authors linking one passage to another, and a regex edge is our reading of 'see part 22.15.7' in the prose. 359 of the corpus's edges are the first and 34 are the second, and until ingest/0.8.0 both were stored as bare strings with nothing to tell them apart.

certainty.description: For regex edges. 'default' is the convention of SOURCE_NOTES.md §8 — 'part 22.15.7' names Part 22 — applied where nothing competes. 'explicit' is the Manual settling it in its own words: 'part 2.3.1(c) of this chapter' says the digits are this Part's address and not Part 2's. 'ambiguous' is both readings resolving against the inventory with nothing choosing between them; the conventional target is kept because the record has nowhere else to put one, and the flag beside it is what stops it being read as a fact. Route ambiguous to review; never follow it as though it were established.

mention.description: The surface form: the anchor's own words for an href edge, the matched phrase for a regex one. The same debugging aid 'mention' is on a provision, and the thing that makes a wrong edge findable.

headings.description: One entry per heading in 'heading_path[2:]', outermost first — the depth of each ancestor, how it was found, and the chunk that holds it. 'heading_path' is a list of strings and so cannot say any of the three. The ancestor's text is deliberately NOT repeated here: it is heading_path[2:][i], and validate.py pins the correspondence over the whole snapshot so that one ancestry cannot become two disagreeing copies of itself.

level.description: Depth, on one scale for both kinds of heading: the digit of an h2-h4, and for an inferred heading the number of components in the number the Manual printed — '3.1' sits where an h3 sits and '3.1.1' where an h4 does. This is what heading ancestry is keyed on, and without it a consumer cannot see the nesting the chunker read, which matters on the three pages where the Manual's numbering and its markup disagree (SOURCE_NOTES.md §28).

source.description: As 'heading_source', but for every ancestor rather than the leaf alone. A chunk can be cut on an h3 while sitting under a heading that was promoted from a bold paragraph, so filtering the corpus to heading_source == 'markup' does not by itself give you an ancestry the Manual marked up.

ref.description: The chunk_ref of the chunk holding this heading's own section, or null where it holds none. Null is the ordinary case for a heading whose content lives entirely in its subsections (SOURCE_NOTES.md §27), and 899 chunks have at least one such ancestor. It is what makes the heading tree addressable: the parent of a chunk is the last entry before it with a ref, and the page where there is none. Where a section was long enough to split, this is its opening fragment, which is where a link to the heading is aimed.

blocks.description: The paragraphs and list items 'text' was flattened from, in document order. Same argument as 'tables', applied to the prose: joining every block's text with single spaces reproduces 'text' exactly, so this is not a second copy of the words — it is the shape the Manual set them in, which flattening destroys. Without it a ten-item list of statutory exceptions and a single paragraph are the same string. Derived from element names and tree depth alone; nothing here reads the words.

kind.description: The element the block was set as. 'heading' is an h5 or h6 — h2-h4 are chunk boundaries and h1 is the page title. 'image' is an img the CMS left loose in a layout div, and is the only kind with no 'text'. 'text' is inline content left loose the same way, and is the fallback for any element not otherwise named.

text.description: Verbatim, whitespace-normalised, and for a list item its own words only — the items nested under it are their own blocks and are not repeated here. Absent on an 'image' block and present on every other kind: an image contributes no words, and a block carrying an empty string would put a stray space into the join that reconstructs the chunk.

depth.description: How many lists enclose a list item, from 1. Present only on 'list_item'. The corpus nests three deep at most; without it a sub-item reads as a sibling of the item it qualifies.

src.description: The img's src, verbatim and usually site-relative. Present only on 'image'. The bytes are not in the snapshot — this records that an image sat at this point in the prose, which the page record's 'images' cannot say.

alt.description: The img's alt text. Present only on 'image', and only where the Manual wrote one — which across 169 images it never has. Absence means the source is silent, and nothing here invents a description.

links.description: Every hyperlink in this chunk, in document order, with the offsets into 'text' where the Manual set it. 'provisions' and 'internal_refs' record what a link means and only where the extractor can say so — an AustLII provision href, or an href naming a page in the nav — deduplicated, sorted, and with the href itself discarded. 792 of the corpus's 2,218 in-chunk anchors reach neither: TimeBase and Federal Register links to the same Acts, WIPO and jade.io, and 47 internal links naming Manual pages that are not in the nav. This is the anchors themselves, verbatim and positioned, which is the only form in which the passage can be read back as the Manual set it. Not deduplicated: two links to one target are two links.

href.description: The href exactly as written — root-relative for a Manual page, absolute for everything else. Resolving one against the site root, or against the nav, is a join the consumer can do; rewriting it here would make the record something other than what the source says. Same rule as an image's 'src'.

text.description: The anchor's own words, and equal to text[start:end]. May be empty: five anchors in the corpus hold no words at all, and one of them is where TMA1995/s42 on Part 32A.1 comes from, so dropping them would lose a citation the pipeline already reads.

start.description: Offset into 'text' where the anchor's words begin. With 'end' this is what lets a reader put the link back where the Manual had it — matching on the anchor's words instead would be ambiguous in the 91 places where one chunk sets the same words as a link twice.

end.description: Offset into 'text' just past the anchor's words. Equal to 'start' for an anchor with no words, which records the point it sat at.

emphasis.description: Every italic, bold, underlined and superscript stretch of this chunk, in document order, with the offsets into 'text' where the Manual set it. The same field 'provision.units[].emphasis' has always carried on the legislation side, and the same argument 'links' makes: flattening to text is the correct verbatim reading of the words and destroys what the markup asserted around them. 437 of the corpus's 522 case-citation positions are immediately preceded by an italic run holding the decision's party names — against the 18 an anchor can supply — and 695 more italics are instrument titles. Nothing here says a span is a case name or a title: that a name sits beside a citation is an adjacency a consumer can walk, and asserting the two belong together is a merge, which belongs downstream. Not deduplicated and not sorted: document order is the Manual's own order, and two spans of the same words are two spans. One record per element and never a merged weight — HTML nests where Word does not, so 1,271 spans are co-extensive with another ('Trade Marks Act 1995'), and collapsing them into a synthetic 'bold-italic' would invent something the source does not have.

kind.description: The element, verbatim. The Manual's own choice between '<i>' and '<em>', or '<b>' and '<strong>', is not normalised: it is a fact about the markup, and the pipeline has nowhere to put the claim that the two mean the same thing. 'sup' is a footnote marker — SOURCE_NOTES.md §26 establishes that a superscript is never a heading number, a fact the chunker has always acted on and never recorded.

text.description: The element's own words, and equal to text[start:end]. Empty spans are dropped, unlike in 'links': an anchor with no words still records a place the Manual put a link, while an '<i>' around nothing asserts nothing about any words.

start.description: Offset into 'text' where the emphasised words begin. Checked corpus-wide by the validator, not in a test alone: an offset drifted by one emphasises the wrong words while staying well-formed.

end.description: Offset into 'text' just past the emphasised words.

tables.description: The grid of every table in this chunk, in document order. 'text' renders a table as a run of cell text — the correct verbatim reading, and no use to anything that needs to know which cell sat under which column. Empty on the great majority of chunks.

ordinal.description: Position among the tables in this chunk, 1-based.

columns.description: Widest row, counting spanned columns rather than cells: a two-cell row whose first cell is colspan=2 is three columns wide.

header_row.description: Index into 'cells' of the header row, or null when the markup does not say. Only <thead> and an all-<th> first row count. The Manual marks up 2 of its 121 tables that way, so this is usually null — the first row is NOT assumed to be a header, because that is an inference about meaning and rule 1 forbids it.

cells.description: Rows of cells, in document order, including the header row if there is one — it is indexed by 'header_row', never copied. Ragged rows are recorded as they are; the grid is not padded out to a rectangle.

text.description: Cell text, verbatim and whitespace-normalised. Empty for a cell holding only an image — the image is on the page record.
